title: Diagnosing the need for agile and its benefits
blurb: Explain from the scenario's facts why agile suits a project, and name the benefit that being and doing agile would bring.
question: Draycott's prediction model needs months of real sensor data before it is reliable. Why does that make agile a good fit, and which benefit would it bring?

teach.body: Formally: complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely one solution that meets every need and covers every risk; it is better to stay adaptable and able to pivot than to spend effort hunting for a perfect answer. In plain English: when you cannot know the right answer up front, build a little, learn from real use, and change course quickly. That is the case the exam wants you to make from the scenario's facts.

teach.h: Benefits of doing AND being agile
teach.body: Doing agile (frameworks, events, techniques, terms) gives structure and can bring short-term efficiency. Being agile (thinking in an agile way and being allowed to act on it within agreed self-management) brings adaptability, a cultural shift and long-term resilience. A common misconception is that adopting a framework guarantees faster delivery or higher quality; the value lies in shifting mindsets so teams can self-manage and decide.

At Draycott Precision Engineering, the data science lead Hannah Reece warns that maintenance records are incomplete and the model needs months of real data. Nobody can specify the perfect dashboard now. Release 1 fits sensors to ten machines so the team learns whether the data is useful: a feedback loop (responsiveness and innovation). Engineers co-design screens and the team decides how to build them (engaged people), while the 98% availability goal stays stable (vision).

teach.text: Classic traps: 'agile is needed because it is faster and cheaper' is the framework misconception, not a reason. Waterfall's main limit is that it cannot adapt during the process. In Table 2.3, 'understanding' is about user needs and 'adaptability' is about changing course; do not swap them.

items: Need for agile: complexity and uncertainty mean the answer emerges from feedback (2.4).
Benefits (2.4): organizational resilience and alignment; efficient teams and engaged people; responsiveness and innovation.
Table 2.3: vision (stable goal), understanding (user needs), adaptability (change course quickly).
Doing agile gives structure; being agile gives lasting change. A framework alone guarantees nothing.

summary: You can now point to the facts in a scenario that show why agile is needed, such as uncertainty, late quality checks or changing needs. You can also name the benefit that being and doing agile would bring and reject the claim that a framework guarantees results.

A.q: At Draycott Precision Engineering, the data science lead warns that the failure-prediction model will need several months of real sensor data before its predictions are reliable, and that the old maintenance records are inconsistent. The operations director asks why the project should be agile. Which explanation BEST fits these facts?
options: Agile frameworks speed up delivery, so the model will be reliable before the aerospace contract starts
The right solution will emerge from real feedback, so staying adaptable beats fixing a design now
Agile lets the team start building before any business justification for the sensors exists
Agile removes the need for management stages, so the board can review the model once at the end
A.why: Complexity creates ambiguity, so there is rarely a single perfect solution; staying adaptable and able to pivot is better than searching for perfection (2.4). The model's uncertainty is exactly this situation.

whyNot.0: Adopting a framework does not guarantee faster delivery; that is the classic misconception (2.3).
whyNot.2: Every PRINCE2 Agile project still needs business justification; agile does not remove it.
whyNot.3: PRINCE2 Agile keeps management stages; the board authorizes one stage at a time.

A.q: During Draycott's first release, the software team is trusted to decide how it builds each dashboard feature, and maintenance engineers sit with the developers to design the screens. After three sprints the team reports higher morale and more stories completed. Which benefit of agile does this show?
options: Organizational resilience and alignment
Responsiveness and innovation
More efficient teams and engaged people
Vision, a goal that stays stable
A.why: Collaboration in cross-functional teams and empowering them to self-manage build trust, ownership and purpose, raising morale and productivity: more efficient teams and engaged people (2.4).

whyNot.0: Resilience and alignment is about navigating change while serving organizational objectives, not morale from self-management.
whyNot.1: Responsiveness and innovation comes from feedback loops and continual improvement reducing waste.
whyNot.3: Vision is a Table 2.3 quality (a stable overarching goal), not a benefit of self-managing teams.

A.q: Draycott's board keeps the target of 98% machine availability unchanged for the whole twelve months, while the software team changes which dashboard features it builds after each shop-floor trial. Which Table 2.3 quality does the unchanged availability target illustrate?
options: Vision
Understanding
Adaptability
Transparency
A.why: Vision is an overarching goal that stays stable for a certain time (Table 2.3); the availability target is that stable goal while the route to it changes.

whyNot.1: Understanding means a deep grasp of underlying user needs.
whyNot.2: Adaptability describes the changing features, not the stable target.
whyNot.3: Transparency is a characteristic of the agile mindset (2.6.2), not a Table 2.3 quality.

B.q: Engineers trialling Draycott's live dashboard say the vibration alerts fire too often to be useful. In the next sprint the team changes the alert logic and drops a planned weekly report that nobody had opened. Which benefit of agile is this MOST LIKELY to show?
options: More efficient teams and engaged people
Responsiveness and innovation
Organizational resilience and alignment
Understanding of underlying user needs
B.why: Feedback loops and continual improvement let teams refine their approach, reduce waste and find innovative solutions: responsiveness and innovation (2.4).

whyNot.0: That benefit centres on self-management, trust and morale, which the stem does not describe.
whyNot.2: Resilience and alignment is about adapting to change while serving organizational objectives across the organization.
whyNot.3: Understanding is a Table 2.3 quality, not one of the benefits; the stem describes acting on feedback.

B.q: Draycott's production manager tells the project board: 'Once the software team is using Scrum, faster delivery and better quality will follow by themselves.' What is the BEST response from the project manager?
options: Scrum improves speed but not quality, so the quality manager must check each release
The benefits come from the framework, so the whole business should adopt Scrum events
Fixing the full scope early is what makes Scrum fast, so features should be frozen now
A framework does not guarantee benefits; they come from a mindset where teams self-manage
B.why: Assuming that adopting a framework guarantees faster delivery or higher quality is a common misconception; agile's value lies in shifting mindsets and empowering teams to self-manage and decide (2.3).

whyNot.0: This still treats the framework as delivering results by itself, and invents a split between speed and quality.
whyNot.1: Spreading events without the mindset is doing agile without being agile.
whyNot.2: Agile protects value by flexing scope, not by freezing all features early.

B.q: Before building any alerts, Draycott's software team spends two days on the shop floor learning what engineers need to know, and how early, before a machine fails. Which Table 2.3 quality is the team building?
options: Adaptability
Vision
Understanding
Collaboration
B.why: Understanding is having a deep understanding of the underlying user needs (Table 2.3).

whyNot.0: Adaptability is the ability to adapt to goals quickly within a bigger strategy.
whyNot.1: Vision is a stable overarching goal, such as the availability target.
whyNot.3: Collaboration is a mindset characteristic (2.6.2), not one of the Table 2.3 qualities.

C.q: Draycott's board suggests running Smart Maintenance as a waterfall project: specify every dashboard screen and every prediction rule during initiation, then build and test everything once near the end. Is this an appropriate way to approach the project, and why?
options: Yes, because fixed time and cost need a scope that is fully fixed at the start
Yes, because the aerospace quality system requires approval before changes are used
No, because PRINCE2 Agile does not allow detailed planning during initiation
No, because waterfall cannot adapt during the process and these needs are uncertain
C.why: Waterfall's main limitation is that it does not allow adaptability during the process (2.2). With an uncertain model and unclear needs, the solution has to emerge from feedback (2.4).

whyNot.0: In PRINCE2 Agile, time and cost are fixed precisely so that scope can flex.
whyNot.1: Quality approval is a real constraint, but it does not justify specifying everything up front.
whyNot.2: Initiation still plans the project; the issue is fixing every detail and testing late.

C.q: To win support, Draycott's project manager tells the board: 'Agile will let us cover all 60 machines faster and more cheaply than the plan.' Is this an appropriate way to explain the need for agile, and why?
options: Yes, because agile teams can minimize waste and reduce delays
Yes, because frequent releases can bring some benefits earlier
No, because adopting agile does not by itself guarantee faster delivery
No, because agile projects flex time and cost to protect the scope
C.why: A common misconception is that adopting agile guarantees benefits such as faster delivery (2.3). The case for agile here is uncertainty and the need to adapt from feedback.

whyNot.0: Agile can reduce waste and delays, but that does not make a promise of guaranteed speed and savings appropriate.
whyNot.1: Earlier benefits are possible, but this does not support promising full coverage faster and cheaper.
whyNot.3: Time and cost are fixed in PRINCE2 Agile; scope is what flexes.

C.q: Draycott's software team has used Scrum for a year. The project manager proposes that the maintenance engineers simply adopt the same Scrum events and terms, with no coaching, so the shop floor 'is agile' by Release 1. Is this an appropriate way to gain the benefits of agile, and why?
options: Yes, because doing agile gives engineers a structure for their work
Yes, because shared terms help the engineers and the developers to work together
No, because doing agile alone may bring short-term gains, not lasting change
No, because the engineers are outside the delivery teams of the project
C.why: Doing agile alone focuses on mechanics and may bring short-term efficiency but lacks sustainable impact; being agile brings the cultural shift and long-term resilience (2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Doing agile does give structure, but without the mindset it does not deliver lasting benefits.
whyNot.1: Shared terms help, but copying events and terms is not enough to change how people think.
whyNot.3: The engineers form a team that defines and trials the dashboard, so they are part of delivery.

reteach.title: Find the uncertainty, then name the benefit
reteach.question: Can you justify agile from the scenario and match the benefit?

blocks.body: First, find the facts that make the answer uncertain: unclear user needs, untested technology, a model that must learn from data. That is why agile is needed. Second, match what the scenario stresses to a 2.4 benefit: change and objectives (resilience and alignment), self-management and morale (engaged people), feedback and less waste (responsiveness and innovation).

blocks.text: A framework does not guarantee faster delivery or higher quality. Vision, understanding and adaptability are Table 2.3 qualities, not the 2.4 benefits.

explain.body: Complexity leads to ambiguity, so a single perfect solution is rarely available. Stay adaptable and pivot quickly instead. Waterfall's limit is that it cannot adapt during the process.

test.q: Draycott does not yet know which sensor readings will predict failures, or what engineers will act on. Which statement BEST explains why an agile approach suits this?
options: Agile guarantees the prediction model will work by the end of Release 1
Agile lets the team learn from real use and pivot when the data surprises them
Agile delivers the full specification earlier than a waterfall plan would
Agile lets the team skip testing until the model has enough real data
test.why: With ambiguity, it is better to stay adaptable and pivot quickly than to look for a perfect solution up front (2.4).

whyNot.0: Agile guarantees no particular result; it manages uncertainty through feedback.
whyNot.2: The point is not delivering a fixed specification sooner; the specification is not knowable yet.
whyNot.3: Agile checks quality early and often; it does not postpone testing.

explain.body: Organizational resilience and alignment (navigate change while prioritizing work that serves objectives). More efficient teams and engaged people (collaboration, self-management, trust, morale). Responsiveness and innovation (feedback loops, continual improvement, less waste).

test.q: When a new aerospace customer brings forward its start date, Draycott's teams reprioritize the backlog so the machines that customer's parts depend on are covered first. Which benefit of agile does this BEST show?
options: Organizational resilience and alignment
More efficient teams and engaged people
Responsiveness and innovation
Adaptability as a Table 2.3 quality
test.why: Agile teams navigate change and adapt while prioritizing work that contributes to organizational objectives, which makes the organization resilient (2.4).

whyNot.1: That benefit is about self-management, trust and morale.
whyNot.2: That benefit is about feedback loops and continual improvement producing innovative solutions.
whyNot.3: Adaptability is a Table 2.3 quality; the question asks for a benefit of agile.

explain.body: Vision: a goal that stays stable for a while. Understanding: deep knowledge of users' underlying needs. Adaptability: adapting to goals quickly within a bigger strategy.

test.q: After a trial shows engineers ignore the energy screen, Draycott's team quickly switches the next sprint to failure alerts, still within the company's maintenance strategy. Which Table 2.3 quality does this show?
options: Vision
Understanding
Respect
Adaptability
test.why: Adaptability is the ability to adapt to goals quickly within a bigger strategy (Table 2.3).

whyNot.0: Vision is the stable goal, not the change of direction.
whyNot.1: Understanding is about grasping user needs; the stem describes changing course.
whyNot.2: Respect is a mindset characteristic (2.6.2), not a Table 2.3 quality.

explain.body: Doing agile gives structure and short-term efficiency. Being agile gives adaptability, a cultural shift and long-term resilience. Benefits come from the mindset, not from adopting a framework.

test.q: A Draycott director asks what the business will gain if staff are allowed to think and act in an agile way, rather than just following Scrum events. Which answer BEST describes the benefit of being agile?
options: A cultural shift and long-term resilience
A clear set of events and shared terms
Short-term efficiency from new routines
A guarantee of higher-quality products
test.why: Being agile leads to a cultural shift and long-term organizational resilience (2.3.1).

whyNot.1: Events and terms are what doing agile provides.
whyNot.2: Short-term efficiency is what doing agile alone may provide.
whyNot.3: No approach guarantees higher quality; that is the framework misconception.
